subject: Tarnmoor GPU Secondary Market Monitor (Oct 14): used 8-GPU H200 server listings jump at three refurbishers - small sample, flagging for awareness
body:
TARNMOOR HARDWARE DATA | Secondary Market Monitor | Week ending Oct 11

Headline datapoint: Listings of used 8-GPU H200-class HGX servers across the three refurbishers/brokers we scrape most reliably rose to 212 units this week from 154 last week (+38% w/w) and from a trailing 8-week average of 131. Listings of H100-class systems were roughly flat at 389.

What we can see:
- Median asking price for H200 8-GPU systems fell 6.4% w/w to an indexed 83 (Jan 2026 = 100). Asks on H100 systems were unchanged.
- 61% of the new H200 listings came from a single refurbisher whose inventory page mentions "lease return" on 40+ units. We cannot tell whether those units came from one seller or several.
- Two of the three brokers added "Blackwell trade-in credit" banners in the last 10 days. Neither was present in September.

How to read this (we do not know yet):
1) Benign: early fleet refresh by GB200/GB300 adopters rotating older capacity out. This would be consistent with strong Blackwell demand.
2) Less benign: financing-driven sales by a smaller GPU cloud or leasing vehicle. If so, it could soften used-GPU residual values.
3) Noise: one large lot hitting the market. Weekly counts in this panel have swung 25%+ before and mean-reverted within two weeks.

Caveats: Panel covers 3 sellers (about 40% of the secondary volume we can observe). Listings are not transactions, we have no sell-through data, and we have not verified serial numbers or end-user provenance. We will refresh next Tuesday and add a fourth broker if onboarding clears.

We are not drawing a conclusion on Nvidia demand from one week of listings, but clients tracking used-GPU residuals asked to be told about step changes. Full CSV attached; the seller-level breakdown is available under the Pro tier.

Dana Okonkwo-Reyes
Tarnmoor Hardware Data
reason: A one-week jump in used H200 server listings with falling asks could signal early Blackwell fleet rotation or financing stress at smaller GPU buyers, and either reading bears on NVDA demand and residual values. The panel is thin, the listings are not transactions and one seller dominates, so it is an unconfirmed signal to monitor rather than thesis-changing.

sender: Naomi Brandt, Cloud & Internet Channel Research, Calloway & Dunn Securities
subject: AMZN: AWS reseller/MSP billing panel points to Sept-quarter acceleration - we raise 3Q AWS rev to $41.5bn (Street ~$40.3bn)
body:
CALLOWAY & DUNN SECURITIES | Cloud Channel Checks | Oct 14

AMZN: AWS channel checks point to upside - raising 3Q AWS estimates, introducing 4Q view

What we did: We aggregated September billing data from 9 AWS resellers and managed service providers. Together they bill about $2.4bn annualized through AWS Marketplace and consolidated-billing arrangements. Two are large enough to be top-10 partners in North America. We compared Jul-Sep against Apr-Jun and against the year-ago quarter.

What we found:
- Panel billings: +26% y/y in the Sept quarter, vs. +21% in June. The acceleration was broad and not driven by one customer.
- Mix: GPU/accelerator instance and inference-related spend (managed model endpoints, vector database, data pipeline) rose from 14% of panel billings to 19% in the quarter. Core compute and storage grew +18% y/y, up from +16%.
- Commitments: Four of the nine partners report average enterprise commit size up 12-20% on renewals. They attribute this to AI workloads moving from pilot to production. None reported commit downsizing at scale.
- Capacity: Three partners said they were told to expect GPU instance wait times through December. This looks like a supply limit, not a demand one.

Estimate changes (preliminary):
- 3Q26 AWS revenue to $41.5bn (+25.8% y/y) from $40.1bn. Consensus is ~$40.3bn (+22.1%).
- AWS operating margin 3Q to 34.4% from 35.2%, on higher depreciation from the AI build and early Trainium ramp costs. Consensus is ~35.0%.
- 4Q AWS revenue to $44.8bn (Street ~$43.2bn).
- Consolidated 3Q operating income to $21.6bn (from $20.9bn). Consensus is ~$20.7bn.

Caveats: The panel is small relative to AWS ($130bn+ annualized) and skews toward mid-market and digitally native customers. Partner billing can lead or lag recognized revenue by up to a month, so treat this as direction, not a point estimate. We would not extrapolate the growth rate to large enterprise.

Bottom line: If AWS prints around +25%, it would be a 3-point beat on growth, partly offset by a margin shortfall vs. the Street. Rating Buy, PT $262 (from $255).

Naomi Brandt | Calloway & Dunn Securities
Full panel table and partner breakdown attached. Disclosures at callowaydunn.com/disclosures.
reason: Differentiated channel-check data with specific numbers (panel billings +26% y/y, AWS 3Q revenue $41.5bn vs. consensus ~$40.3bn, margin and 4Q changes) ahead of the Oct 29 print. Concrete estimate changes that could move AMZN expectations make it thesis_relevant, despite the small, mid-market-skewed sample.

sender: Federal Register Watch - Daily Alerts
subject: IMPORTANT: Court of Appeals vacates Interior Dept. grazing-permit renewal rule; agencies must reissue guidance within 120 days
body:
FEDERAL REGISTER WATCH | LEGAL ALERT | Oct 14, 2026

U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit vacates federal rangeland grazing-permit renewal rule

Summary: In a 2-1 opinion issued Tuesday, the Tenth Circuit vacated a 2024 Interior Department rule that streamlined renewal of grazing permits on federal rangeland. The court held the agency failed to conduct adequate environmental review under NEPA before adopting categorical exclusions for renewals of ten-year permits.

Key holdings:
- The rule is vacated nationwide; remand to the agency without vacatur of existing permits already renewed under the rule.
- The majority said the agency 'did not adequately explain' why renewal impacts on sage-grouse habitat could be treated as categorically insignificant.
- The dissent argued the agency's analysis was entitled to deference.

What happens next:
- Interior has 120 days to reissue guidance on pending renewals (approx. 2,300 permits).
- The agency could seek rehearing en banc or file for certiorari; the deadline for rehearing petitions is Oct 28.
- Ranchers' associations said they expect delays in renewals in 11 western states.

Who is affected: Livestock operators holding federal allotments, state land boards, conservation groups, and agricultural lenders with exposure to western ranch credit.

Full opinion (62 pp.) and docket link: fedregwatch.org/10thcir-grazing

You are receiving this alert because your keyword profile includes 'court' and 'federal rule.' Manage alerts here.

Summary: In the past 10 days we spoke with 9 authorized resellers and regional electronics chains (5 in the U.S., 2 in Japan, 2 in Germany) about their holiday-quarter Apple allocations. - Sample size is small and skews to mid-sized resellers, who are typically the first to see allocation changes
- No quantification from Apple. Cuts could be a re-weighting toward direct (Apple retail, online) channels
- Two of the resellers said their iPhone allocations had risen, which could offset some of this
- Wearables plus iPad are roughly 15-17% of AAPL revenue, so even a true 10% cut at resellers would be a modest figure at the company level

Why it's on our radar: Last year, a similar pattern preceded a December-quarter wearables result that came in about 2% below consensus. This year's checks are too thin to draw the same conclusion.

Next steps: We are adding 10-12 more reseller calls this week and will check with two distributor contacts in Asia. We will update by Monday.

Hartfield Gray Research | Internet & E-commerce | Short note

AMZN (Buy, PT $270 unchanged)

No estimate changes. One observation from our pre-print work that we think the Street is not yet reflecting.

We have been tracking local planning filings, lease commencements and job postings for Amazon's same-day delivery sites (the smaller, near-metro facilities that sit between fulfillment centers and last-mile stations). Our count shows 31 sites commencing operations in the December quarter, against 17 in the same quarter last year and about 20 in our earlier model. Many of them appear to have been pulled forward from Q1 2027 rather than added.

Why it matters: these sites carry pre-opening and ramp-up costs, with underutilized labor and rent for the first 8-12 weeks. Using management's past commentary on regionalization startup costs, we estimate $0.9-1.3bn of incremental Q4 operating expense versus our prior assumption. Revenue should not get much of a lift in the quarter, as the benefits from lower cost-to-serve and faster delivery accrue mostly in 2027.

Implication for the print: The Street's Q4 operating income guide midpoint sits near $22.0bn (our model: $21.6bn before this change). We now think a guide that brackets the Street range at the low end is more likely than one at the high end. We would view a soft Q4 OI guide driven by this investment as consistent with a stronger 2027 cost-to-serve, but it would be unfavorable for near-term estimates and positioning.

We will say more after Oct 29.

Marguerite Oyelaran | Hartfield Gray Research

sender: Dr. Ingrid Solheim, Head of Asia Macro Research, Brandtwood Global Markets
subject: Korea Macro: Household debt, the BoK's Oct 22 meeting and why we expect a hold with a dovish tilt
body:
BRANDTWOOD GLOBAL MARKETS | Asia Macro Research | Oct 14

Bank of Korea: hold on Oct 22, but the bias is shifting

Summary: We expect the BoK to keep the base rate unchanged at 2.75% on Oct 22 (vote 5-2, with two members preferring a cut). The forward guidance language is likely to soften from 'maintain restrictive stance' to 'assess the timing of adjustment'.

Key drivers

1) Household debt. Household credit rose 0.4% m/m in September, the slowest monthly pace since early 2024, as macroprudential limits on mortgage lending in the capital region took effect. The debt-to-GDP ratio has stabilized near 90%. This reduces the central bank's financial-stability argument for holding.

2) Inflation. Headline CPI printed 1.9% y/y in September, with core at 2.0%. Rent and public-service prices are the main drivers; goods inflation is subdued as the won has firmed 2.6% against the dollar since July.

3) Growth. Exports grew 3.8% y/y in September on a working-day-adjusted basis. Domestic demand remains soft: retail sales -0.6% m/m. We keep 2026 GDP growth at 1.7% and 2027 at 1.9%.

4) Housing. Seoul apartment prices rose 0.3% m/m, a deceleration from the 0.7% pace in July. Transaction volumes fell about 18% m/m.

Market implications
- We see 2 x 25bp cuts by mid-2027, with the first in Q1.
- 3-year KTB yield target: 2.55% (from 2.65%).
- USD/KRW: we expect a range of 1,340-1,380 through year-end.
- Equity: no direct view; foreign flows are being driven by the global rate path.

Risks: a faster-than-expected rebound in Seoul housing; a sharp won depreciation if U.S. yields rise further.

Raj, Marcus,

A quick note from our Taiwan/Shenzhen contacts. This is early and unconfirmed. We are sharing it now because the timing sits ahead of Nvidia's November print.

What we heard (4 of 9 add-in-board partner and distributor contacts, over the last 10 days):
- The mid-cycle refresh of the Blackwell desktop line (higher-capacity memory SKUs) was pencilled in for a holiday-season launch. Four contacts now say the target has moved to "Q1, maybe CES."
- Two of the four cited GDDR7 allocation. One said the larger memory modules are being prioritized for professional and data center-adjacent boards, and that this is "not a yield issue."
- Channel inventory for current-generation mid-range cards is described as "healthy to slightly heavy" at two Shenzhen distributors. One said they have asked partners to slow October shipments.
- Three of the other five contacts said they had heard nothing about a delay. One said holiday SKUs are on schedule.

Why it might matter: we model gaming at roughly 8-9% of FQ3 revenue. A delayed refresh would mostly shift timing and mix within gaming. It would not change the data center picture. The more interesting angle is whether memory is being reallocated toward higher-margin products, but that is our inference, not something any contact told us.

What we don't know: no contact has seen formal communication from Nvidia. Two of the four are the same distributor group, so the count of independent sources is closer to three. The sample is small and skews to partners that sell mid-range cards.

Next steps: we will re-check with the three remaining AIB partners after Oct 21 and will flag if the picture firms up. No change to our estimates or rating.

Happy to talk through it if useful.

Dana Whitlock
Hardware Channel Research | Penhallow Securities
For institutional clients only. Based on unverified industry conversations.

subject: South Africa: SARB's new 3% target era - why November looks like a hold and what the rand is pricing
body:
IRONVALE SECURITIES | EM Strategy | South Africa Rates & FX
Oct 14, 2026

Summary: We expect the SARB to hold the repo rate at its Nov 19 meeting. Our view is that the central bank will stay cautious as it settles into the lower 3% inflation target adopted earlier this year. The rand looks fairly valued to us on near-term fundamentals and is supported mainly by firm precious-metal prices.

Data points:
- September CPI printed 3.1% y/y (consensus 3.2%), with core at 3.4%. Services inflation is sticky at 4.0%, driven by administered prices (electricity, municipal tariffs).
- Inflation expectations of businesses, from the quarterly survey, are 4.3% for 2027. That is still above the new target and is the main reason we think the Bank will avoid cutting.
- The primary budget surplus is tracking 0.9% of GDP for the fiscal year, slightly ahead of the February plan. Debt-service costs still absorb roughly 21 cents of every rand of revenue.
- The current account is in a small surplus (0.4% of GDP) on mining export prices.

Markets: USD/ZAR trades near 17.40. We see a 17.00-18.00 range into year-end. The 10-year bond yield is at 9.3%, and the 2s10s curve slope is 220bp. We would stay overweight 10-year bonds against a 5-year fixed-rate payer, a carry-and-roll trade with modest convexity.

Risks:
- A reversal in gold and platinum prices would hit the terms of trade quickly.
- A weaker-than-planned Medium-Term Budget Policy Statement (due Oct 28) would steepen the curve.
- Rising grid-maintenance costs could push administered inflation higher.

What would change our view: two consecutive core prints below 3.2% would bring a cut in Q1 2027 into play.

Nomvula Dlamini
EM Strategist | Ironvale Securities

Not research, just color from my own calls this week. I know you like the odd customer-tone datapoint ahead of the print.

I spoke with 11 corporate IT/procurement contacts since Monday (all Azure customers with multi-year commits). Three of them volunteered, without prompting, that their Microsoft account teams have recently been much more accommodating on commit terms:

- Global industrial manufacturer: offered a 9-month extension of its Azure consumption commitment window with no true-up penalty. Procurement lead said, "A year ago they would not have discussed it."
- Regional bank: told it could roll an expected ~$6-8m shortfall into the next agreement at current discount tiers. Their burn-down is running a bit behind plan because two migrations slipped.
- Large specialty retailer: the rep proactively raised "migration credits" and flexible rollover for unused commit. The CIO's read was that Microsoft wants to protect the renewal rather than push for a larger commit.

The other eight said nothing had changed, and two of them said Azure teams are still pushing hard on AI workloads and capacity reservations.

How I'd frame it: this could just be normal post-quarter-end behavior. The September fiscal quarter-end has passed, reps are clearing renewals, and shortfall rollovers are common enough. But all three described it as a change versus prior cycles, and the common thread is customers consuming more slowly than they committed. That sits a bit awkwardly next to the capacity-constrained, demand-exceeds-supply narrative into the Oct 28 print. It is a small sample, and none of the three are among the biggest consumers.

I'll ask our software analyst whether his partner checks show the same thing, and I'll update you if I hear it from more accounts. Happy to put you on with any of the three if you want to hear it directly (they're customers, not former employees, so no expert-network paperwork).

sender: Marianne Okafor, Investor Relations, Alphabet Inc.
subject: Alphabet Inc. - Notice of change in accounting estimate: server and network equipment useful lives (effective Oct 1, 2026)
body:
Dear Investors and Analysts,

Ahead of our third quarter 2026 results on October 27, we are notifying you of a change in accounting estimate that will be reflected in our Q3 financial statements and Form 10-Q.

Summary of the change
Following a review of the service lives of our technology infrastructure, we are reducing the estimated useful life of certain AI-accelerated servers and associated networking equipment from six years to five years, effective October 1, 2026, on a prospective basis. The review took into account the pace of hardware refresh cycles for AI training and inference workloads. Useful lives for other servers, data center buildings and land are unchanged.

Expected financial effect
- Depreciation expense in Q4 2026 is expected to increase by approximately $0.7 billion relative to the prior estimate.
- For full-year 2027, we currently estimate an increase in depreciation expense of approximately $3.9 billion, depending on the pace of capital deployment.
- On an after-tax basis, we estimate this to reduce diluted EPS by approximately $0.26 in 2027.
- The change is non-cash and has no effect on capital expenditures, cash flow or our previously communicated investment plans.
- The impact will be allocated across Google Services and Google Cloud segments in proportion to equipment use. We expect Google Cloud operating margin to be affected more than Services.

Prior periods will not be restated.

We will provide additional detail, including segment-level effects, on our October 27 call. Please direct questions to the Investor Relations team after the call and not before, so that all investors receive the same information at the same time.

This notice is also being furnished on Form 8-K.

Marianne Okafor
Investor Relations
Alphabet Inc.

This communication contains forward-looking statements, including estimates of future depreciation expense, which are subject to risks and uncertainties.

sender: Neil Ashby, Director of Strategic Accounts, Quillfish Data
subject: Marketplace commit drawdowns - odd pattern we're seeing into Q4
body:
Raj,

Something I wanted to share because I haven't heard it discussed on your side. Treat this as color from one vendor rather than a data point you can model off.

We sell observability and data pipeline software, and our deals are increasingly closing through the AWS and Microsoft marketplaces. Of the 14 deals we closed in the last six weeks, 9 were transacted through a marketplace. Our reps tell me the buyers' procurement teams have mostly been asking the same thing: 'can this count against our committed spend?'

What's different this quarter is why they're asking. In 5 of the 9 marketplace deals, the customer told us directly that their cloud consumption is running 10-20% behind their annual commit (EDP on AWS, a MACC on Azure), and they want to buy software to burn the commit down before it expires, rather than pay a shortfall. Two of those customers pulled purchases forward from next fiscal year. One large customer renegotiated its AWS commit lower at renewal last month and mentioned an optimization project that cut compute spend by about a fifth. Another said its Azure commit true-up was pushed to the next period, which they described as 'a relief.'

Why it might matter: when a customer burns commit through a marketplace purchase, the cloud provider generally books only its marketplace fee on that purchase, not the full contract value. So commit can be satisfied with less revenue flowing to the hyperscaler than a straight compute burn would produce. If this is widespread, it points to customers who are growing cloud usage more slowly than they planned a year ago. It would also mean the commit backlog numbers look healthier than the revenue conversion is.

What I don't know: whether our customers are representative (they skew to mid-to-large enterprises, many of which are optimization-minded), or whether any of this reaches the reported numbers. I have no visibility into the providers' own reporting.

I'm happy to share more detail on the nine deals, with names removed, if that helps.

Neil
Quillfish Data | (415) 555-0126

subject: AMZN / NVDA: EC2 Capacity Block scrape - GB300 availability widening, short-term pricing softer (early, 2-week data)
body:
BRAMWELL OSTROW RESEARCH | Cloud Infrastructure | Early Read (not a rating change)

AMZN, NVDA: Is GB300 capacity at AWS loosening?

Summary: Our daily scrape of EC2 Capacity Blocks (the short-term reservation product for GPU clusters) shows a notable change in availability and pricing for GB300 (P6e) instances over the last two weeks. This is early and the sample is small, but we want to flag it ahead of AMZN's October 29 print and NVDA's November report.

What we observed (scrape of 9 AWS regions; 14 days through Oct 12)

Metric | Late Aug | Oct 12
Regions with GB300 blocks bookable at under 48hr lead time | 2 of 9 | 7 of 9
Median lead time for a 64-GPU, 7-day block | 19 days | 4 days
Implied $/GPU-hr (median across regions) | $7.12 | $6.34 (-11%)
H200 blocks, same metric | $3.88 | $3.71 (-4%)

Three customer conversations (two AI start-ups, one enterprise research group) said AWS account teams offered shorter minimum terms on newer clusters. One said that was new relative to the summer.

Possible explanations
1. Supply: more GB300 racks landing at AWS than planned, which is consistent with the stronger Blackwell Ultra ramp checks we and others have seen and would be positive for both AWS revenue and NVDA shipments.
2. Demand: smaller buyers (start-ups, neoclouds) pulling back on short-term GPU rental as funding tightens. That would show up in AWS GPU utilization rather than in NVDA's hyperscaler orders.
3. Mix: AWS may be steering short-term demand to its own Trainium instances, which we cannot see in this data.

Caveats: 14 days is too short to determine a trend. Capacity Blocks are a small fraction of AWS GPU revenue (most capacity is committed or on-demand), and price changes could reflect list-price adjustments not tied to utilization. We have no company confirmation.

What would change our view: A second month of data, AWS commentary on capacity on the Oct 29 call, or secondary-market GPU rental quotes moving in the same direction.

No estimate changes. We keep the scrape running and will update in two weeks.

Callum Reyes | Bramwell Ostrow Research
Disclosures available at bramwellostrow.com/disclosures
reason: Early, two-week scrape data suggests GB300 capacity at AWS is easier to book and priced lower, which could mean either faster supply (positive) or softer short-term GPU demand (negative) for AMZN and NVDA. The sample is small, covers a minor part of AWS GPU revenue, and the analyst makes no estimate changes and cannot say which explanation is right. This is a credible emerging signal worth tracking rather than a thesis-changing finding.

subject: GridSense AI Load Index (Sept): metered IT load at 140 AI halls - non-hyperscaler utilization falls to 63%, Hopper-to-Blackwell migration slower than modeled
body:
Hi Larchmont Ridge team,

Our September AI Load Index is out. The headline finding runs against the prevailing "everything is sold out" narrative on AI compute for non-hyperscaler customers.

Method: We read sub-metered IT power draw at 140 AI-designated data halls (47 operators) across 9 U.S. and European markets and convert it to a load factor, meaning measured draw divided by contracted critical power. Halls are classified by the accelerator generation reported by the operator or our sensor mapping.

September results (load factor, vs. June):
- All AI halls: 63% (June: 74%)
- Hyperscaler-operated halls (n=38): 82% (-1pt)
- Neocloud and colo AI halls (n=71): 54% (June: 71%)
- Enterprise/sovereign halls (n=31): 49% (June: 58%)

By accelerator generation:
- Hopper halls: 41% (June: 66%)
- Blackwell/GB200 halls: 80% (June: 83%)

Why this matters: Hopper capacity at neoclouds is going idle faster than the market assumes. 22 of 71 neocloud halls show load below 40% for three consecutive weeks. Idle Hopper capacity reduces the incentive to buy Blackwell racks and strains the financing behind existing fleets. The Street's FQ3/FQ4 Nvidia models assume non-hyperscaler data center revenue grows about +9% q/q, in line with the commentary from management. Our data is consistent with flat to down, and we would flag the growth assumptions for neocloud and enterprise demand as most at risk. Hyperscaler loads remain full.

Caveats: Load factor is not a perfect proxy for utilization (reserved but idle capacity can still pay). 26 halls had sensor gaps, and November data will help confirm.

The full dataset (hall-level, anonymized) and a methodology note are attached. We can walk your team through the data on a call this week.

Best,
Nadia Ferreira
Head of Research | GridSense Analytics

TICKER WIRE | TECHNOLOGY | Oct 14, 8:12am ET

Nvidia CEO reiterates Rubin timeline, touts sovereign AI deals in Washington keynote

Nvidia's chief executive spoke for about 50 minutes yesterday at a public AI policy and industry summit in Washington. The keynote was webcast and is available on demand. Key points as reported:

- Rubin: Management said the platform remains "on track" for volume shipments in the second half of calendar 2026, matching what the company said on its August earnings call.
- Sovereign AI: He highlighted three previously announced government-linked projects (in Europe, the Middle East and Southeast Asia) and said demand from national programs "continues to broaden." No new customers or dollar figures were provided.
- Supply: He described the supply chain as "tight but improving," the same wording used in prior public commentary.
- Export controls: He said the company would continue to "work with the administration" on licensing and did not comment on pending Commerce rulemaking.

sender: The Long Ledger - Issue 38 (Editor: Maren Holloway)
subject: The Long Ledger #38: Merrivale Surety - why the boring bond business earns a 19% ROE
body:
THE LONG LEDGER | Issue 38 | Deep-Dive Edition

Merrivale Surety Group (privately held filings; trades OTC as MRVS) - the underwriter nobody watches

Surety bonds are a niche insurance product: a contractor posts a bond guaranteeing project completion, and the surety steps in if the contractor defaults. Merrivale is a top-10 U.S. writer with $2.3bn of direct written premium, and we think the market undervalues its economics.

The unit economics
- Combined ratio (5-yr average): 79%, versus 97% for commercial P&C peers. Surety losses are rare but severe, and underwriting standards (not pricing) are the main lever.
- Loss ratio in 2025: 21%. The loss ratio was above 30% only once in the past 12 years, in the 2009 downturn.
- Return on equity: 19% through the cycle, with minimal reserve volatility. Reserve development has been favorable in 11 of the last 12 years.

Why the moat is durable
- Bond underwriting depends on contractor financials and relationships. Merrivale has a 27-year average broker tenure.
- Infrastructure-law funding means public-project bonding demand has risen; Merrivale's public-works book grew 14% in 2025.
- The company keeps capital-light reinsurance on its large accounts, limiting tail risk.

Risks
- A large contractor default (a $200m+ project) could produce a single-year loss ratio shock of 8-10 points.
- Pricing pressure from new entrants backed by private capital.
- Concentration: top 20 principals account for 22% of premium.

Valuation
At $41/share, MRVS trades at 11.5x our 2027E EPS of $3.56 and 1.9x book. Peers with lower returns trade at 1.8-2.2x book. Our base case of $54 assumes 6% premium growth and a 82% combined ratio. A bear case at an 88% combined ratio and 3% growth gives $37.

Bottom line: A well-run underwriter with a defensible niche and a clean balance sheet. Full 11-page model available to paid subscribers.

The Long Ledger | Independent research for long-term investors

HARBOURGATE SECURITIES | Asia Semiconductors | Channel Check | Oct 14, 2026

NVDA (Buy): China data center revenue risk looks larger than consensus assumes

Bottom line: Our latest round of checks suggests that Chinese hyperscaler and internet-platform orders for Nvidia's China-compliant Blackwell-class accelerator are being put on hold, and in a few cases cancelled, following informal guidance to buyers. Consensus models roughly $2.5bn per quarter of China data center revenue from FQ4 (Jan quarter) onward. We think that number is at risk of going to near zero.

What we checked (Oct 6-13): 6 distributors and system integrators in Shenzhen and Hong Kong, 2 Taiwanese server OEM account managers, 1 data center procurement manager at a large Chinese internet platform.

Findings:
- Four of six channel contacts said at least one top-5 Chinese internet customer has deferred a pending purchase order for the compliant part. The reason given was verbal guidance from regulators to "prioritize domestic accelerators for new capacity."
- The procurement manager said her company's 2027 inference expansion is now being planned primarily around domestic parts, with Nvidia limited to training clusters that were already approved.
- One OEM account manager said about 40% of the FQ4 allocation of finished compliant units had been unwound or put on hold. The other said volumes were "flat to slightly lower" than the August plan, so not all checks agree.
- Reallocation offset: Contacts expect any freed-up CoWoS and HBM supply to go to non-China demand, but with Blackwell Ultra and Rubin already sold out through 2027, we see limited near-term revenue offset.

Estimate sensitivity: Removing $2.5bn of quarterly China revenue is about 2.8% of our FQ4 revenue estimate of $89bn and roughly $0.05 of quarterly EPS at our modeled margins. Gross margin would also lose a modestly dilutive product, so the percentage-margin effect is slightly positive. The bigger issue is narrative. Bulls have framed China as free upside to numbers that already exclude it, but our checks suggest it is in the Street's numbers.

Caveats: Sample is small, guidance is informal and the policy has reversed before. We would want one more round after the Oct 28 company-level meetings.

We maintain Buy but cut our FQ4 China assumption to zero from $2.0bn. See our model update this afternoon.

sender: Dana Whitfield, Director of Federal Affairs, Tallwood Policy Group
subject: AI training-data: expedited appeal + Senate discussion draft - early read for the whole megacap group
body:
Ellen, Raj,

A quick heads-up from DC. Nothing here is final and I would treat it as a slow-burn item, but two processes are moving at the same time and both reach the same group of companies.

1) Appeals track. The appellate court hearing the lead consolidated fair-use case on AI model training granted a motion to expedite last week. Briefing closes in December and argument is being discussed for late January. Defendants and amici across the consolidated matters include Microsoft (Copilot and its model partner), Alphabet (Gemini-family training sets), and Amazon (Nova models and Alexa+). Separate author suits name Apple (on-device model training data) and Nvidia (the NeMo/Megatron training corpora). Each defendant's facts differ, and the district court rulings so far have split on market-harm arguments. A ruling before Q2 is unlikely.

2) Senate discussion draft. Judiciary subcommittee staff are circulating a bipartisan discussion draft that would require disclosure of training-data sources above a compute threshold and set up an opt-out registry for rightsholders. Comments from industry are due Nov 20. Staff told us they do not expect a markup this year, and the draft may be folded into a broader AI package.

Why it matters (possibly): A ruling for the plaintiffs, or a disclosure mandate, would raise data-licensing costs and could affect how each company labels and sources its training data. The largest exposure sits with the firms that publish consumer-facing generative products. Companies that mainly supply hardware or tools are less exposed, but not immune. The trade groups are quietly preparing a joint comment letter, which is the first sign they take the draft seriously.

What I do not know: the likely scope of the compute threshold, whether the draft preempts state rules, and whether any defendant is negotiating a settlement. The licensing deals each company has signed may blunt the effect.

None of this changes Q3 numbers. I'll send the comment letter and the court's scheduling order once I have them. Happy to talk it through.

Dana
Tallwood Policy Group | Washington, DC
reason: A policy contact flags an expedited appeal on AI training-data fair use and a Senate disclosure draft that could raise data-licensing costs, with all five targets named as defendants or affected parties. The process is early, the timing is uncertain, and there is no near-term earnings impact, so it fits monitor rather than thesis_relevant.

AAPL, GOOGL: carrier merchandising tone is shifting into Q4

Over the last ten days we spoke with seven people responsible for device merchandising or retail inventory: three at national carriers, two at regional carriers and two at big-box electronics chains. Our standard questions on holiday plans produced a different tone from what we heard in July and in last year's equivalent round.

For Apple, the relevant question is whether carriers' more cautious ordering reflects true sell-through softness or just a leaner inventory stance.

BOSPHORUS & VALE RESEARCH | EM Macro | Turkey

CBRT Oct 22 preview: a 100bp cut, with the guidance doing the work

Bottom line: We expect the central bank to cut the one-week repo rate by 100bp to 38.0% on October 22. The statement should keep the 'tight stance for as long as necessary' language and stress that monthly underlying trends, not the headline, drive decisions.

The data:
- September CPI printed 2.4% m/m (annual 33.8%), above the 2.1% consensus. Services contributed 1.3pp, with rent and restaurants sticky.
- Our seasonally adjusted underlying trend is ~2.1% m/m, still too high for the year-end target path.
- The ex-ante real policy rate (vs. 12m-ahead expectations) is about 9.5%, down from 12% in Q1.

External side:
- Net reserves ex-swaps recovered ~$14bn since June, helped by tourism receipts and eurobond issuance.
- The 12m current-account deficit is about 1.4% of GDP, and the energy bill is the swing factor.
- Foreign holdings of lira government bonds have rebuilt to ~$9bn from a $2bn trough.

Market view: Lira carry remains attractive on a risk-adjusted basis (3m implied vol ~14%), but the trade is crowded. We expect USD/TRY at 44.5 by year-end, in line with the forward-implied depreciation, so carry mostly compensates rather than generates excess return. A surprise 150bp cut would likely steepen the curve and weaken the lira by 2-3% on the day.

Risks: Wage indexation in January, administered price hikes in energy, and a global risk-off episode.

Selin Aktuna | Bosphorus & Vale Research

subject: China consumer policy: early word that the smartphone trade-in subsidy may be wound down at year-end (single source, unconfirmed)
body:
Raj, Marcus,

Flagging something from our Shanghai team that we have not seen anywhere else yet. We are treating it as an early, unconfirmed signal, not a call.

What we heard: A contact at a provincial commerce bureau (someone who has been reliable on prior subsidy mechanics) said a internal draft is circulating that would let the national consumer trade-in program for phones and other electronics lapse after December rather than extend it into 1H27. The same draft reportedly considers redirecting remaining central funds to appliances and EV scrappage. He was explicit that nothing has been approved and that two other provinces still want an extension.

Why it matters for Apple: The program subsidizes 15% of the retail price on handsets, with a per-unit cap, for models priced under 6,000 yuan. Most Pro-tier iPhone configurations sit above that threshold and benefit only partially via the capped amount, but the base and Plus models, plus older-generation iPhones sold through carriers, benefit fully. Our channel survey from September suggested roughly a third of mainland iPhone sell-through in the quarter touched the program in some way. If the subsidy ended in January, the pull-forward into the holiday quarter could be followed by a soft Mar-quarter comp in Greater China.

What we do not know:
- Whether the draft is a real policy path or one bureau's wish list
- Whether the Politburo's year-end economic meeting (usually mid-December) changes the consumption messaging
- How much of Apple's Greater China holiday-quarter guide already assumes subsidy support. We think the Street has not explicitly modeled it either way.

Macro context: Retail sales of communication equipment grew 11% y/y in August vs. 24% in June, which is consistent with the subsidy fading at the margin. Our house view remains that consumption support will be incremental, not large-scale.

What we are watching: State Council executive meeting readouts, any NDRC notice on 2027 funding allocations, and carrier promotion calendars in November. We will update if a second source emerges.

Happy to discuss on a call this week.

Hi Ellen,

Our rates strategy team published a short piece this week that I thought might be useful for your macro framing, and I'd like to show you the tool behind it.

The observation: the 5y5y forward inflation swap has drifted to 2.62% while the household 5-10 year expectations survey has fallen to 3.4%. The gap between market-implied and household expectations is now about 78bp, the narrowest since early 2022 on a survey-minus-market basis. Historically, when the gap compresses this quickly, core services inflation has been stickier for the next two to three quarters (median +0.15pp vs. the prior trend in our sample of 9 episodes since 1998).

What we think it means:
- The market is pricing a cleaner disinflation path than households are experiencing at the checkout.
- Term premium is absorbing most of the adjustment, with 10-year yields moving more on supply than on inflation news.
- A hot November CPI would likely move front-end pricing more than long-end breakevens.

Caveats (we're upfront): survey data are noisy, the sample of episodes is small, and the 2022 episode is doing a lot of work in the median.

sender: Philip Okonjo, Head of Consumer Macro Strategy, Tarrant & Wills Global Markets
subject: Consumer Macro: Lower-income cohort pulling back at Amazon - Sept card panel shows basket-size cuts, trade-down to Prime-only buys
body:
TARRANT & WILLS GLOBAL MARKETS | Consumer Macro Strategy | Oct 14, 2026

U.S. consumer: cracks at the bottom of the income distribution, and Amazon is where it shows first

Our monthly card-panel update (n ~ 1.9m anonymized U.S. credit and debit accounts) shows a notable split in September spending behavior.

Headline: Overall nominal spending was +3.6% y/y, in line with August. The deceleration is entirely in the bottom income tercile, where discretionary e-commerce spend slowed to +0.8% y/y from +3.1% in July.

Amazon-specific patterns (panel basis):
- Average basket size among bottom-tercile Amazon shoppers fell ~6% y/y in September, the first y/y decline in the series since early 2024
- Share of bottom-tercile orders consisting of only Prime-eligible items under $25 rose to 44% from 38% a year earlier
- Order frequency was steady, which suggests shoppers are still transacting but buying less per order
- Top-tercile Amazon spend rose +5.2% y/y, in line with the trend

We also note that bottom-tercile delinquency on retail cards rose 40bp m/m in our panel, and student-loan repayment resumption is hitting the same cohort. Our macro view is that real disposable income growth for the bottom 40% has turned negative for the first time since 2023, helped along by shelter costs and a softening labor market.

Tone shift vs. prior months: In our July and August reports we described low-income spending as "resilient but stretched." We now think it is "deteriorating at the margin." We would not extrapolate from one month, and we are not changing our Q4 retail sales forecast of +3.1% y/y.

Implications for equities: Amazon has the broadest low-income exposure among the mega-cap platforms, mostly through its core retail and Prime ecosystem. A second month of basket compression would raise questions about Q4 unit growth and the holiday guide. We will watch the October panel closely.

Other items: Core PCE nowcast for September is 0.24% m/m; no change to our Fed view (hold in December, one cut in Q1).

Philip Okonjo | Tarrant & Wills Global Markets
reason: A macro strategist reports that card-panel data show lower-income Amazon shoppers cutting basket sizes for the first time in nearly two years, and he explicitly softens his previous tone on consumer resilience. It is a credible but single-month signal with unclear impact on the Q4 guide, so it warrants monitoring rather than immediate action.

subject: Sunbelt Industrial Dispatch (Oct 14): Amazon's real estate team 'back in the market'? Plus cold storage rents, port-adjacent land
body:
SUNBELT INDUSTRIAL DISPATCH | Wednesday, October 14

TOP STORY: Is Amazon's real estate team changing its tone?

For most of the past year, brokers across Texas, Georgia, Arizona and the Carolinas described Amazon's real estate group as being in "digestion mode": few new lease requests, a few lease give-backs, and a clear preference to fill existing capacity first. That may be shifting.

We spoke with nine industrial brokers and two developers this week. Their comments:
- Five of the nine said they received new requirements from Amazon in the past three to four weeks, the first in more than six months. Typical asks are 400,000-1,000,000 sq ft, delivery targeted for second half of 2027.
- Three described the tone as "more urgent" than in the spring. One said the Amazon team asked about power availability and tenant-improvement turnaround times before asking about rent.
- Two of the five said the requests are for same-day and regional sortation formats, not traditional fulfillment centers.
- The remaining four brokers have heard nothing new from Amazon. One noted that requirements are sometimes floated and then withdrawn.

Caveats: This is a small, self-selected sample and requests are not signed leases. Amazon routinely tests the market and has declined to comment on specific site searches. We cannot tell whether this reflects a change in the company's network plan or the usual seasonal pattern ahead of annual budgeting.

Why it matters: Lease commitments typically show up in capex and fulfillment cost lines one to two quarters later. If the requests firm up, they would point to a reacceleration in network build plans for 2027.

ELSEWHERE
- Cold storage: Vacancy in Atlanta tightened to 5.8%; asking rents flat q/q.
- Port-adjacent land: Savannah and Houston sites trading at 12-15% premiums to inland comps.
- Dallas-Fort Worth: Spec construction starts fell for the third straight quarter.

Sunbelt Industrial Dispatch is published weekly. Forward to a colleague or manage your subscription at the link below.
reason: Brokers report that Amazon's real estate team has re-engaged on new 2027 lease requests, which may mean a shift from digestion to expansion and could affect fulfillment capex and cost expectations. subject: The Quiet Compounder #29: Vantine Lift Systems - the service annuity hidden inside an elevator maker
body:
THE QUIET COMPOUNDER | Issue 29 | October 14, 2026

This month: Vantine Lift Systems (VLFT)

The pitch in one line: Investors treat Vantine as a cyclical building-products company. About 61% of its operating profit comes from maintenance and modernization contracts that look more like an annuity.

The numbers
- Revenue FY26: $5.9bn. New equipment 38%, maintenance 46%, modernization and repair 16%.
- Operating margin by segment: new equipment 6%, maintenance 22%, modernization 14%.
- Installed base: about 1.9m units under contract, up from 1.6m in FY21. Portfolio retention is 93%, and the average contract runs 4.1 years.
- Maintenance pricing has risen 3-4% per year since FY22, helped by remote-monitoring upgrades that cut technician callouts by roughly 12%.

Why the market misreads it
Sell-side models tie the valuation to new-equipment orders, which fell 7% in the last twelve months as commercial construction slowed. That order book is mostly a feeder for the service base: each new unit converts to a maintenance contract at roughly an 85% attach rate, and a unit's lifetime service profit is 4-5x its equipment margin.

The risk case
- Technician wage inflation (3.5-4% per year) has to be matched by price. Three of the last 12 renewal cohorts slipped below that line.
- Share loss in Asia: the new-unit price war has pushed Vantine's China market share from 14% to 11% in two years.
- A smaller independent-servicer threat in North America, where independents now hold about 18% of the installed base, up from 14%.

Valuation
At $212 the stock trades at 19x our FY27 free cash flow estimate against a 5-year average of 23x. If service margins hold at 21-22% and retention stays above 92%, we see about 11% annual free cash flow per share growth through FY29 and a fair value near $265. A retention drop to 90% takes it to roughly $225.

What we'd watch: contract renewal price spreads in the Q1 filing; the Asia modernization backlog; the independent-servicer share.

This newsletter is for information only and is not a recommendation. The editor holds a small position in VLFT.

sender: Wen-Li Chao, Sourcing Network Liaison, Pearl Delta Trade Advisory
subject: AMZN: Shenzhen/Guangzhou sellers say Amazon Haul order volumes slowed in Sept and price-cap guidance changed (6 conversations, anecdotal)
body:
Hi Raj, Marcus,

This is a small-sample check from our sourcing network, so please weight it accordingly. It may be a seller-specific story and not a trend.

What we heard (six conversations with sellers and sourcing agents in Shenzhen and Guangzhou, Oct 7-12; all supply low-ticket apparel, home goods and accessories into Amazon's low-price Haul storefront):

1. Volumes: Five of six described September order volumes as "clearly lower" than August. The magnitude ranged from roughly 15% to 30% m/m. One seller said October is tracking flat to September.

2. Price caps: Three said Amazon's seller guidance now tightens the maximum listed price on some categories (two cited a drop from $20 to $15 on home goods), and one said a minimum-margin rule was applied to listings with high return rates.

3. Logistics: Two sellers said Amazon asked them to consolidate shipments into fewer, larger inbound lots from mid-October. They read this as a cost-control step. One said the change "saves us money" and was not unhappy about it.

4. Competing platforms: Three said they had moved some inventory to rival low-price marketplaces, citing lower fees. Two of those three said Amazon volume remained the larger share.

What we cannot tell you:
- We have no Amazon-reported figures, and sellers do not know Haul's overall share of Amazon GMV. Our guess is that it is small.
- All sellers are Guangdong-based. Sellers in other regions may see a different pattern.
- A seasonal dip around Golden Week (Oct 1-7) could explain part of the September-to-October softness, although it would not explain the August-to-September move.
- We have not heard from Amazon, and this has not been corroborated.

We plan to re-poll the same sellers in about two weeks, plus another 10-12 from a second sourcing hub. We will send an update if the pattern firms up or fades.

Best,
Wen-Li
Pearl Delta Trade Advisory
reason: Anecdotal channel check from six Chinese sellers that suggests softer Amazon Haul volumes and tighter price and logistics rules. It is plausible but unconfirmed, comes from a small regional sample, and has an uncertain link to total AMZN retail. A follow-up poll is planned, so it belongs under monitor.

body:
KINGSFORD CAPITAL | Energy Services | Industry Update | Oct 14

Offshore Drilling: Day rates plateau, but backlog quality improves

Bottom line: Floater day rates have stopped rising, but contract duration and backlog visibility are improving. We stay constructive on the group, favor the owners of high-spec 7th-generation drillships, and name Halvane Offshore (HLVO) our top pick.

What we saw this month:
- Ultra-deepwater fixtures in September averaged ~$448k/day, vs. $452k in August and a $475k peak in Q1. Four fixtures were in the $430-470k band, with terms of 2-3 years.
- Utilization for 7th-generation drillships is 96%. Six 6th-generation units remain warm-stacked, and we expect two to be retired or sold for scrap by mid-2027.
- Brazil: The state operator's tender calendar now shows five floater tenders for 2027 starts. We estimate this adds ~700 rig-days of demand versus 2026.
- West Africa: Two long-term awards (3 years+) were announced. Operators are paying up for dual-BOP capability.

Costs: Crew cost inflation is running at ~4.5% y/y and shipyard reactivation costs are $75-100m per unit, which limits supply response. We think day rates are structurally supported near $425k for modern units.

Halvane (HLVO): Backlog of $5.1bn with 2.6 years average remaining term. We model 2027 EBITDA of $1.18bn (vs. consensus $1.12bn) on better uptime at 97.5%. Net debt/EBITDA falls to 1.9x by YE27, which opens room for a $400m buyback. Our PT is $41 (from $38), based on 6.5x 2027E EV/EBITDA.

Risks: Oil below $60 Brent for a sustained period, operator capex discipline, and rig-delivery slippage at the shipyards.

Marisol Teague | Kingsford Capital Energy Services
Disclosures and analyst certification available on request.

sender: Tomas Reinholt, Head of Data Products, Kelmarsh Cloud Telemetry
subject: Kelmarsh AccelMix Q3 release: Trainium share of NEW accelerated-instance hours at 27% (from 14% in Q2) - Nvidia instance share of new AWS GPU hours falls to 71%
body:
Hi Raj and Marcus,

Our Q3 AccelMix panel has just been finalized, and we are sending it to subscribers ahead of the general release on Friday because the headline moves against the prevailing view on AWS accelerator mix.

What AccelMix measures: instance-level usage metadata from 1,940 enterprise and startup AWS accounts that have opted in through our cost-optimization tooling (about 3.1m accelerated instance-hours per day in September). We classify hours by accelerator family. 'New' hours are those from accounts whose first use of a given instance family was in the last 120 days.

Share of NEW accelerated-instance hours, AWS panel:

| Family | Q1-26 | Q2-26 | Q3-26 |
| Nvidia (H100/H200/B-class) | 88% | 83% | 71% |
| AWS Trainium (Trn2/Trn3) | 8% | 14% | 27% |
| Other (Inferentia, AMD, etc.) | 4% | 3% | 2% |

Share of TOTAL accelerated hours: Nvidia 86% (from 91% in Q2), Trainium 12% (from 7%).

What is different this time:
1. Previous quarters' Trainium growth came mostly from a handful of very large anchor accounts. In Q3, 62% of the incremental Trainium hours came from accounts outside the top 20 by spend, and 41% of those accounts also ran Nvidia instances in Q2. That looks like real migration, not just anchor-customer concentration.
2. Median per-job cost on Trainium for fine-tuning and inference workloads was 34-41% lower than on comparable Nvidia instances, based on the 212 accounts in the panel that tag workloads by job type.
3. Training of frontier-scale models remains almost entirely on Nvidia (97% of hours in jobs above 2,048 accelerators), so the shift is concentrated in the mid-market.

Our read: The common assumption is that Trainium is capped by a few internal and anchor workloads and that Nvidia keeps more than 90% of third-party AWS accelerator usage. Our data suggests otherwise for non-frontier workloads. If the pace holds through Q4, it would favor AWS's own accelerator economics and put pressure on Nvidia's share at its largest cloud partner.

Caveats: the panel skews toward cost-conscious accounts (the tooling is a cost optimizer), which likely overstates Trainium share relative to all of AWS. Reserved capacity commitments made by large customers are not visible to us.

Full tables and methodology are attached. Happy to walk through the cohort analysis on request.

Best,
Tomas Reinholt
Head of Data Products | Kelmarsh Cloud Telemetry
reason: New panel data shows Trainium taking a much larger share of new AWS accelerated hours, driven by broad mid-market migration rather than anchor customers. This challenges the consensus that Nvidia holds more than 90% of third-party AWS accelerator usage and bears on both NVDA share and AMZN's custom-silicon economics. The panel's skew is acknowledged, but the incremental evidence is material.

subject: Rates & Banks: ECB terminal rate and deposit betas - a deep dive on Banco Verdelar's 2027 NII
body:
VALMONT BRANDT RESEARCH | Euro Rates & Financials | Oct 14

ECB on hold through mid-2027: what it means for NII, using Banco Verdelar (VRD SM) as the case study

Bottom line: We expect the ECB deposit rate to stay at 2.00% through at least Q2 2027, with the risks to our call skewed toward an extended pause. In that environment, the debate on bank earnings moves from rate direction to deposit mix. Banco Verdelar is the clearest example in our coverage.

Macro backdrop:
- Euro-area core inflation has settled in a 2.2-2.4% range, and services wage growth is running at about 3.4%.
- Our terminal-rate model puts the neutral rate at 2.0-2.25%, which means little room for cuts without a growth shock.
- The 2y/10y German curve is 78bp, up 20bp since July, which supports reinvestment yields.

Verdelar's NII sensitivity:
- Spanish retail deposits (61% of funding) have a through-the-cycle beta of 28%, but our branch-level data shows beta rising to roughly 36% as term-deposit promotions return in Q4.
- Roughly 54% of the loan book reprices within 12 months (mortgages indexed to 12M Euribor), so a flat ECB means Euribor stays near 2.15%, and NII holds.
- We estimate that each 10pp rise in deposit beta costs EUR 95m of 2027 NII (about 3.4%).
- The bond portfolio (EUR 38bn, duration 2.8 years) rolls over at about 80bp above the running yield, adding EUR 210m to 2027 revenue.

Estimates: 2027E NII EUR 2.79bn (+2.1% y/y), core RoTE 14.6%, CET1 13.4% before buybacks of EUR 1.1bn. Our valuation of 9.8x 2027E EPS and a 7.6% total cash yield is supported by capital generation of about 160bp per year.

Risks: faster deposit competition from digital banks; a Spanish bank tax extension; a weaker credit cycle in consumer lending (cost of risk currently 41bp).

Rating: Overweight. Price target EUR 6.80 (from EUR 6.50).

Valmont Brandt Research | Disclosures at the end of this document.

sender: Lena Hartmann, Head of Swiss and Nordic Macro Research, Alpenrose Capital Markets
subject: Switzerland: SNB December meeting - why we expect a hold at 0% and what a stronger franc means for imported disinflation
body:
Alpenrose Capital Markets | Macro Research | Switzerland

SNB: Zero is the floor of our comfort zone, not the destination

Swiss CPI printed at 0.2% y/y in September (consensus 0.3%), with core at 0.4%. The headline is within the SNB's 0-2% price-stability range but has now been in the bottom quarter of that range for six months, which raises the question of whether the Bank will return to negative rates at its December 10 meeting. We expect a hold at 0%.

What drives the call:
1. Franc strength is doing the work. The trade-weighted franc is up about 3.5% since March. Imported goods prices are -1.8% y/y. We estimate each 1% appreciation shaves ~0.07pp from CPI over 12 months.
2. Domestic inflation is not collapsing. Services inflation sits at 1.1% and rents are rising at 2.9% as the reference rate adjusts. This makes a dovish shift less pressing.
3. The SNB's own forecast. The September conditional forecast had inflation at 0.3% for 2027 and 0.6% for 2028 at a policy rate of 0%. A downward revision in December is likely but probably small.
4. Tools. President-level comments have stressed FX intervention as the preferred first line of defense. We estimate the SNB bought roughly CHF 6bn of FX in Q3, based on sight-deposit data. We expect further purchases before any move back into negative territory.

Market pricing: OIS currently discounts about 8bp of cuts by December and 14bp by March. We think that is too much and recommend receiving only on a break of EUR/CHF below 0.91.

Risks: A sharp equity sell-off driving safe-haven flows into the franc; a faster-than-expected ECB easing path; a surprise in the Q3 GDP release (Nov 27).

Trade ideas: Stay long CHF vs. NOK on carry-adjusted valuation; 2s10s Swiss curve steepener targeting 45bp.

Lena Hartmann | Alpenrose Capital Markets
For institutional clients only. Disclosures at alpenrosecm.com.

sender: Corinne Haldane, Head of Survey Research, Dalloway Economics
subject: Dalloway Cycle Watch (Oct 14): Mid-market CFOs trim tech budgets as financing costs bite - renewals tone harder on software, Mac refresh pushed out
body:
DALLOWAY ECONOMICS | CYCLE WATCH | October 14, 2026

Headline: Mid-market capital spending intentions soften again; technology budgets are not immune

This month's survey (fielded Sept 28 - Oct 9) covers 212 CFOs and IT heads at U.S. companies with $100m-$2bn of revenue. Responses are self-reported and unweighted.

1. Capex intentions. The net balance of firms planning to raise capex over the next 12 months fell to +3 from +11 in July. 58% cite financing costs as the main constraint, up from 47%. This matches the move in long yields over the past six weeks and the tightening in lower-tier bank lending standards in the latest loan officer data.

2. IT budgets. 41% of respondents say they will hold or cut 2027 IT spend in real terms, vs. 33% in July. The cut is concentrated in hardware and in seat-based software. Two items from the free-text section and the cross-tabs are worth flagging:

- Microsoft: 34% of respondents who buy Microsoft 365 say renewal conversations are 'more adversarial' than a year ago. Most describe pushing to reduce seat counts or step down from E5 to E3. 22% say they are deferring or negotiating separately the Copilot add-on rather than bundling it. Several said account teams were 'more willing to move on price than last year.' Only 9% said they plan to expand Copilot seats in the next two quarters.

- Apple: 27% of firms that run mixed Mac/Windows fleets plan to delay their Mac refresh into 1H27, vs. 17% in July. The most common reason given was extending depreciation schedules to preserve cash. Eleven respondents mentioned trimming iPad and iPhone stipends for field staff. None said they were switching platforms.

3. Caveats. The sample is small, mid-market skewed and self-reported. Our January wave also showed a harder tone on software renewals, and that did not obviously show up in reported results for the following two quarters. The Mac and iPad figures rely on a subsample of 88 firms. We would treat this as direction, not magnitude.

4. What we are watching. Microsoft's Oct 28 commentary on commercial bookings and the FQ2 guide, and Apple's Oct 29 Mac/iPad guide. If management tone on renewals and refresh timing matches the survey, we would read the tone shift as real. If not, this is likely noise from rate sensitivity in a narrow segment.

Other items this month: regional Fed manufacturing indices (mixed), small-business hiring plans (net +6), and our updated recession-probability tracker (31%, from 28%).

Full cross-tabs available to subscribers.

Corinne Haldane
Dalloway Economics | Survey Research
To unsubscribe, reply with 'remove'.
reason: A credible but small, self-reported survey suggests customers are getting tougher on Microsoft 365 renewals and Copilot add-ons and delaying Mac refreshes, tied to higher financing costs. That could shift Microsoft and Apple demand expectations, but the sample is thin and the same signal in January did not clearly translate into reported results. It is an emerging, unconfirmed tone shift to monitor into the Oct 28-29 prints.

subject: Ravenmoor Chemicals Weekly: TiO2 price hikes meet resistance; chlor-alkali caustic tightens ahead of winter
body:
RAVENMOOR RESEARCH | CHEMICALS WEEKLY | Oct 14, 2026

Titanium dioxide: second price-increase round meets resistance

Two of the four major producers announced a $120/t increase for Nov 1, following the $100/t round in July. Our coatings and plastics channel checks (14 formulators) suggest roughly 40% of the July increase stuck in North America and about 25% in Europe. Buyers cite inventories of 9-11 weeks and soft architectural paint volumes. We assume $60-70/t realization on the November round, which supports a modest margin tailwind for the integrated producers in 1H27 but is below the producers' public rhetoric.

Chlor-alkali: caustic soda tightening
Operating rates at U.S. Gulf Coast plants are at 82% (vs. 77% in Q2) after two unplanned outages. Caustic spot is up $35/dry ton in two weeks. Alumina refiners and pulp mills are the main buyers; chlorine derivative margins (PVC, epoxy) remain squeezed because of weak housing-related demand. Winter heating season typically cuts chlorine demand and keeps chlor-alkali operating rates tied to caustic pricing.

Specialty additives: restocking, not recovery
Orders for UV stabilizers and antioxidants improved 6% sequentially in September, but our distributor survey points to inventory rebuilding after destocking in 1H. We would not extrapolate to end demand. Auto production schedules and packaging volumes are flat to slightly lower.

Natural gas input costs: Henry Hub at $3.40/MMBtu is 18% above last year. European producers face a TTF-to-Henry spread of roughly $6, which keeps energy-intensive ethylene crackers under pressure.

Estimate changes
- Veltrane Chemical (VLTR): 3Q EPS to $1.18 from $1.22; PT $71 (from $73)
- Orsted Coatings (ORCT): 4Q EPS to $0.64 from $0.61 on better mix; PT unchanged at $48
- Kanmoor Industries (KNMR): no change; Neutral

Our next weekly will include 3Q results previews for the diversified names.

subject: ALERT: China to license exports of gallium, germanium and heavy rare-earth magnet materials from Nov 16; review times up to 45 working days
body:
TESSERA NEWSWIRE | MARKETS ALERT | Oct 14, 08:12 ET

CHINA'S COMMERCE MINISTRY ANNOUNCES EXPANDED EXPORT LICENSING ON KEY ELECTRONICS INPUTS

China's commerce ministry said this morning that exports of high-purity gallium, germanium, gallium nitride and gallium arsenide wafers and epitaxy, and magnets containing dysprosium and terbium above set thresholds will require case-by-case licenses from Nov 16.

Key details from the notice:
- Review period of up to 45 working days per application.
- A fast-track 'general license' for verified end users is mentioned but has no published criteria or start date.
- The ministry cited 'national security and non-proliferation obligations' and did not name countries.
- Existing orders shipped before Nov 16 are not affected.

Market reaction (premarket): Rare-earth producers outside China +4% to +9%; Japanese magnet makers +3%; AAPL -1.1%, NVDA -1.6%; USD/CNH little changed.

Desk context (Tessera analysis):

AAPL: Dysprosium/terbium magnets sit in the Taptic Engine, speakers, MagSafe and camera actuators. Two Japanese magnet suppliers have said in past filings that they hold 8-12 weeks of finished inventory for large consumer electronics customers, which would cover most of the December-quarter build but leave exposure to the March-quarter build if licenses stall.

NVDA: Exposure is indirect. Gallium nitride devices are used in the high-voltage power shelves for rack-scale systems, and germanium goes into some optical components and specialty fiber. Power-supply makers typically carry gallium wafer inventory of roughly one quarter.

What matters: The practical impact depends on how fast licenses are approved and whether Chinese authorities use discretion on US-linked end customers. Positions sized around holiday iPhone builds or rack-level power-component tightness are most sensitive, while those that aren't should treat this as a watch item.

Next: We will update on any ministry clarifications and supplier comments.

Tessera Newswire. Content for subscribers only; not investment advice.

subject: Gas turbine delays said to hit power for a Texas AI campus leased to Microsoft; developer says schedule 'under review'
body:
DATACENTER LEDGER | NEWS ALERT | Oct 14

Turbine delivery slips said to affect Texas campus slated for Microsoft capacity

Three people familiar with the matter, including two working at an engineering and construction contractor on the site, told Datacenter Ledger that delivery of behind-the-meter gas turbines for a ~600MW data center campus outside San Angelo, Texas has slipped by an estimated 6-9 months. The campus is being developed by Corral Peak Digital Infrastructure and is understood to be pre-leased to Microsoft for AI workloads.

What we were told:
- The turbines were ordered from Halvern Power Systems in early 2025 for phased delivery starting in Q1 2027. One source said the first units are now expected in Q3 2027 at the earliest.
- Halvern reportedly cited a shortage of large forged rotor components and testing-bay capacity.
- The utility interconnection for the site is separate and remains on its original schedule, but it would only cover about a third of the planned load.
- Phase 1 shell construction is continuing, but one contractor source said some electrical fit-out work has been 're-sequenced'.

Company responses:
- Corral Peak said its 'delivery schedule is under review as is normal for a project of this scale' and declined to comment on equipment suppliers.
- Halvern said it does not discuss customer orders.
- Microsoft did not respond to a request for comment.

Caveats: We could not independently confirm the new delivery dates. Microsoft's capacity in the region may also be met by other sites and its lease terms could include delay provisions. We are not aware of any change to Microsoft's capex plans.

Why it matters: Power equipment lead times are one of the main gating items for new AI capacity, and slippage at one site would be a small part of Microsoft's pipeline but could be an early sign of broader turbine bottlenecks.

We will update as more details emerge.

Datacenter Ledger | Reporting on the buildout of digital infrastructure
reason: An unconfirmed but multi-source report that turbine delays could push out power for a Microsoft-leased AI campus. The data-center power constraint is a plausible emerging signal for MSFT capacity, but the companies decline to confirm and it affects a single site, so it is a monitor item.

sender: Gwen Halvorsen, Beverages & Spirits Analyst, Marlowe Crane Securities
subject: Spirits: TTB final rule on nutrition and allergen labeling - compliance dates, cost math and what it means for mid-cap distillers
body:
MARLOWE CRANE SECURITIES | Beverages & Spirits | Regulatory Update

TTB publishes final rule on "Alcohol Facts" labeling

The Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau published its final rule in today's Federal Register requiring a standardized nutrition-style panel and major-allergen disclosure on wine, distilled spirits and malt beverage labels.

Key provisions:
- Mandatory "Alcohol Facts" statement (serving size, calories, carbohydrates, fat, protein) for all covered products.
- Major-allergen statement required where applicable (e.g., finings in wine).
- Compliance date: 36 months from publication for large producers; 60 months for small producers (under 250,000 gallons annually).
- Voluntary QR-code option allowed for the detailed panel, but the headline calorie and serving information must remain on-pack.

Cost framework (our estimates):
- One-time relabeling and artwork cost per SKU: $2,500-$6,000.
- Large spirits producers (average 150-400 SKUs): $0.5-2.0m one-time, spread over the compliance window, less than 0.1% of annual revenue.
- Smaller craft distillers: proportionally heavier, around 0.6-1.2% of annual revenue for those with narrow volumes.

Our view: Compliance costs are manageable for the large players and are largely a non-event for FY27-28 earnings. The more interesting second-order effect is competitive: small craft brands may face SKU rationalization, which could help distributor mix over time. We see no change to demand elasticity.

Coverage actions: No changes to ratings or price targets. Top picks remain Hartwell Spirits (HWSP) and Brenmoor Wine Estates (BRWE).

Gwen Halvorsen | Marlowe Crane Securities
Important disclosures and analyst certification available at marlowecrane.com/disclosures.

MERIDIAN EXPERT NETWORK | Transcript Summary | Call date: Oct 12, 2026

Expert: Former VP Data Center Deployment at a top-5 U.S. GPU cloud operator (left August 2026). Previously 6 years at a hyperscaler.
Interviewer: Meridian client (buy-side, TMT)

Key takeaways (summary prepared by Meridian; full transcript attached):

1. Deployment pace. The expert said his former employer brought roughly 140,000 GB300 GPUs into production in the September quarter, versus an internal plan of about 110,000. He attributes the beat to improved rack-level yields from the ODMs and fewer liquid-cooling leaks than in the first GB200 ramps.

2. Rubin pre-orders. The operator placed a 2027 Rubin-class order that he described as "about 2.3x the size of our GB300 commitment by GPU count," with delivery windows starting in the second quarter. The expert said it had been confirmed with Nvidia in September with a deposit, and that allocation was "better than we expected given everyone is asking."

3. Pricing. Nvidia did not offer meaningful discounts on the order. "They did not need to. We were told other buyers were queued behind us." He said his former employer accepted a modest price increase on the networking bundle.

4. Demand backdrop. Customers are signing three-to-five-year take-or-pay contracts at rates he described as "stable to slightly up" for H200-class instances, which he sees as evidence that inference demand is absorbing older capacity.

5. Risks flagged. Power availability, not chip supply, is now the binding constraint at the operator's two largest sites. He said he sees no sign of order cancellations at peers.

sender: Dana Whitcombe, Commercial Vehicle Analyst, Corrington Securities
subject: Trucks: NHTSA final rule mandates automatic emergency braking on Class 8 tractors by MY2030 - content-per-truck math for suppliers
body:
CORRINGTON SECURITIES | Industrials | Industry Update

IMPORTANT: Federal safety agency publishes final rule on heavy-truck AEB

The federal vehicle safety agency released its final rule yesterday requiring forward-collision warning and automatic emergency braking on new Class 8 tractors, with compliance beginning in model year 2030 (September 2029 production). The rule was largely in line with the 2024 proposal. The main changes are a lower test-speed threshold for loaded vehicles and a one-year phase-in for vocational tractors.

Key provisions:
- Systems must stop or mitigate impact at closing speeds up to 40 mph on dry pavement
- Radar-plus-camera fusion is effectively required, since camera-only systems struggle with the stopping-distance tests
- Small-volume manufacturers (under 1,000 units a year) get an extra 12 months
- Agency estimates compliance cost of about $1,150 per tractor, vs. our supplier-based estimate of $1,400-1,600

Supplier read-through:
- Brake-control and radar suppliers see the largest content uplift. We estimate $600-800 of added content per tractor for the lead system suppliers, on roughly 250k U.S. tractor builds a year.
- Aftermarket retrofit demand is limited because the rule applies only to new vehicles.
- Truck OEMs should recover most of the cost through pricing, but fleets may pull forward orders into MY2029 to avoid the first compliant units.

Financial impact: We add roughly 40bp to 2030E content growth for our two brake-systems names and leave 2027 estimates unchanged, because the revenue sits outside our forecast window.

Ratings and price targets unchanged. We continue to prefer the radar-exposed names over the pure mechanical brake suppliers.

Dana Whitcombe | Corrington Securities
Disclosures available on request.

sender: Nathan Okafor, Director, Trade & Customs Checks, Harbourgate Policy Research
subject: Trade counsel check: CIT remand on tariff-refund mechanics - hearing Nov 4; protest deadlines and replacement-tariff drafting (9 conversations)
body:
Larchmont Ridge TMT desk,

Following our spring work on tariff exposure, here is the latest from nine conversations this week with customs brokers, in-house trade counsel and two former CBP officials. It is a developing legal process and some of it is early. Please treat it as a flag, not a conclusion.

What is happening:
1. The Court of International Trade has scheduled a remand hearing for Nov 4 on how refunds would work if the emergency-powers tariffs are finally held unlawful. The issues are who can claim, whether protests on liquidated entries must already be on file, and how interest is calculated.
2. Three brokers say CBP has told large importers informally to preserve protest rights on entries liquidating after mid-November. Two said they have seen no such guidance.
3. Two counsel with Treasury contacts say staff are drafting replacement tariffs under alternative statutory authorities, so that any refund would come alongside narrower, more durable duties. Timing is unclear and may slip until after the midterms.

Why it touches all five names (exposure depends on importer-of-record status, which is not disclosed):
- AAPL: iPhone and Mac imports have been the most tariff-sensitive. Large product categories carried exemptions, so refund potential is hard to size.
- AMZN: acts as importer of record on a share of first-party goods and devices. Third-party sellers largely carry their own duties.
- MSFT and GOOGL: Surface, Xbox and Pixel hardware, plus server and networking gear for data centers.
- NVDA: Systems assembled by ODMs in Taiwan and Mexico, so it matters who is the importer of record.

Our read: Possible one-time refund gains, but also a risk that replacement duties are broader. Net effect on estimates is unclear, and the macro angle (goods inflation, import prices) is plausible but unquantified.

What we are watching: the Nov 4 hearing, any CBP notice on protest procedures, and Federal Register entries for new statutory tariff actions.

Nathan Okafor
Harbourgate Policy Research
reason: Channel checks on a developing court process over tariff refunds and possible replacement duties, with plausible but unquantified effects on all five companies and goods inflation. Sources conflict and timing is uncertain, so it is a credible early signal to monitor rather than a confirmed thesis change.

subject: AMZN: Possible free-returns policy test via drop-off fees - early reports from 3 states, unconfirmed
body:
Brindlewood Securities | Consumer Internet | Early Read

AMZN: Are returns getting a price tag? Small test, thin evidence

What we saw: Over the past nine days we found 11 shopper posts (two retail-deal forums and a local-news comment thread) describing a $1.99 "drop-off processing fee" applied at checkout of the return flow for certain apparel and home items returned to carrier-run drop-off points. Reports cluster in Ohio, Arizona and North Carolina. Returns picked up at the door, or dropped at Amazon-owned locations, reportedly remain free. Two of the four seller-support contacts we spoke with said they had seen a new fee line in return-cost reports, but neither could say how many ASINs were affected.

What we don't know: Amazon has not commented and we have not yet raised this with IR. We can't rule out an A/B test, a seller-funded fee, or a display glitch. The sample is tiny, and several posts lack screenshots.

Why it could matter: If extended, a modest fee could shift returns toward Amazon-owned drop-off, where processing costs are lower, and trim reverse-logistics expense. Rough math: ~25% of U.S. returns go via third-party drop-off; a $1.99 fee on that share, at roughly 40% collection, is worth about $300-500m annually. The bigger unknown is conversion and Prime-sentiment risk, which is why the policy has historically been left alone.

What we're doing: No change to estimates or rating. We will watch for (1) confirmation from a seller-facing help page, (2) wider geographic spread, and (3) any comment on the Oct 29 call about returns costs or customer-friction tests.

Nathan Okafor | Brindlewood Securities
This is a preliminary note and not a full research report. Disclosures available on request.

subject: Cockpit RFQs - noticing a pattern with Google's in-car assistant (FYI, personal view)
body:
Hi Raj,

Good to catch up at the supplier dinner last month. A small observation from our side that I thought might be useful given your Alphabet work. Please don't quote me. This is my read of our own pipeline, not an official view of Rivenhall.

We make infotainment and digital cockpit modules for a handful of global automakers. Over the past ~10 weeks, four of the seven open cockpit RFQs we have in hand (two European, one Japanese, one Korean OEM) have specified Android Automotive with Google built-in AND a Gemini-based in-car assistant as a baseline requirement for model years 2028-29. In the prior cycle, only one or two of the RFQs we saw did this, and most left the assistant 'open'.

A few other details:
- Two of the OEMs asked us to price the Google services licensing as a separate line item, which suggests they expect the per-vehicle fee to be negotiated directly with Google.
- One OEM also asked about an on-board compute upgrade (about 2x NPU capacity) to run parts of the assistant locally, with cloud fallback.
- Two OEMs that previously talked about building their own assistant stacks have gone quiet on it.

What I can't tell you: how much Google collects per vehicle, whether the cloud-inference piece is billed to the OEM or bundled, or how many of these programs actually reach production. Automakers re-scope cockpit programs all the time, and these decisions are 2-3 years from revenue. It's also just four RFQs.

But the direction is consistent: the OEMs seem to be accepting Google's stack in return for faster time to market. If it holds across more programs, it's a quiet adjacent revenue line for Alphabet (Services licensing, plus some Cloud inference).

Happy to give an update if the pattern continues once the next two RFQs close in November.

sender: Dominic Aldrete, Chief Strategist, Harlan Reach Macro Research
subject: China export deflation and cross-border ad budgets: early, unconfirmed signal for Google's APAC retail vertical
body:
Ellen, Raj, Marcus,

Short early-read note from our China/EM desk that sits between macro and the ad names. Please treat it as unconfirmed.

Setup: China's export prices have now fallen for 11 straight months. Margins at cross-border merchants selling into the U.S. and Europe are thin, and yuan-side input costs are not falling as fast as selling prices. Two of our contacts, a Shenzhen cross-border payments processor and a Hong Kong agency reseller that buys media on behalf of Chinese merchants, independently told us this week that merchants have started trimming overseas performance-ad budgets for Q4.

What we have:
- Processor: remittances from ~1,900 merchant accounts to overseas ad platforms were down ~7% in September vs. August (their own figure, not audited). August to September is normally flat to up as holiday budgets are set.
- Reseller: 3 of its top 10 merchant accounts asked to cap daily budgets through December, mostly in Shopping/Performance Max-style formats. Two other accounts raised budgets. Net direction is down, but the sample is tiny.
- Our export-price nowcast: the manufactured-goods subindex fell 0.6% m/m in September, which supports tighter merchant economics. It does not prove a budget response.

What we do not have: platform-level confirmation, any split between Google, Meta and TikTok, or evidence that this is a net decline rather than a shift to marketplace-native ad tools. The processor also skews to mid-sized merchants, who are more price-sensitive than the large exporters.

Why it might matter for GOOGL: Street estimates for China-based advertisers' share of Alphabet's ad revenue run from high single digits to low double digits, and the company does not disclose it. A broad 10% cut in their Q4 spend would be worth roughly 70-110bp of Q4 ad revenue. It has not been broad so far.

Our take: not enough to change estimates. We will ask the processor for October data after the 20th and revisit. On Alphabet's Oct 27 call, the APAC retail commentary is worth listening for.

Dominic Aldrete
Chief Strategist | Harlan Reach Macro Research
reason: A macro strategist relays two independent but tiny and unaudited data points suggesting Chinese cross-border merchants are trimming overseas ad budgets, which could modestly pressure Google's Q4 ads revenue. The signal is credible but unconfirmed, with no platform-level data, so it fits monitor rather than thesis_relevant.
